title: Quantum computing's exponential speedups are likely an idealization artifact

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Quantum computing's exponential speedups are likely an idealization artifact

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Although the usual formalism of quantum mechanics allows constructing quantum computers that could solve some problems exponentially faster than ordinary Turing machines, this will likely not reflect ultimate physical reality but only idealizations in current models.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I strongly suspect that even if this is formally the case, it will still not turn out to be a true representation of ultimate physical reality

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Undecidability and Intractability” (from p. 753), p. 771. Scope: quantum computation and the fundamental physics of our universe

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-28: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.46

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Current quantum-hardware data test implementations and noise models, not whether all exponential speedups fail fundamentally. Resolving the physical hypothesis requires qualitatively larger, controlled devices or a new physical theory with discriminating predictions.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define physical scale and error thresholds at which fault-tolerant quantum computation should retain asymptotic speedup, then compare increasingly large devices with classical algorithms and physical-noise models. Sustained error-corrected scaling would count against the claim; a reproducible fundamental breakdown unexplained by engineering limits would support it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Ultimate physical reality is not finitely operationalized.

Engineering failure cannot establish a fundamental physical limit.

Present devices are far below asymptotic regimes.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Published quantum-advantage experiments are real public data about whether present devices outrun classical simulations on contrived tasks. They leave open whether exponential quantum speedup is an artifact of the model or a feature of physical law: the tasks, the noise, and the moving classical competition all fit both readings. The experiments probe a proxy for the claim about ultimate physical reality.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare asymptotic runtime of the best physical quantum device with the best classical algorithm on a problem whose classical cost is exponential under standard assumptions. A sustained exponential gap on a fault-tolerant device would challenge the claim that the speedup is only an idealization; matching classical scaling once those idealizations are dropped would support it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Failure to build a fault-tolerant machine is compatible with the quantum formalism being physically correct.

Later classical algorithms have narrowed several claimed speedups.

A noisy device beating a classical sampler on one task leaves ultimate physical law open.
